title: A hymn in Vadhans
hook: a wedding song about a horse and a lament that begins with praise, a few pages apart

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Vadhans: peacocks in the rain, and wedding songs and laments in one raga. Your line was joy and grief.

What's the first word of a funeral song? In Guru Nanak's laments in Raga Vadhans, it's blessed. A few pages earlier in the same raga, the music is for a different scene: a horse groomed and saddled in a lane strung with lights, relatives singing, the groom climbing on, the drum starting up. Today, one song of each.
screen: `A LAMENT THAT BEGINS: BLESSED.` → `A HORSE IN A LANE OF LIGHTS.` → `ONE RAGA, BOTH SONGS.`

segments.voice: First, the wedding. Guru Ram Das's ghorian, the songs of the wedding horse, start with a surprise of their own. The horse isn't a horse. In plain English: this body is the mare, and the Lord made it. Blessed is the human body, the song says, gained by good fortune. Then it puts on the saddle of understanding what is good, and rides the mare across the hard road toward the Lord. The groom's ride to the bride's home becomes the soul's ride toward God. Anyone who has seen a groom set out has the picture already; the Guru only changes who's riding where. Now the lament. Guru Nanak's alahnian open, in plain English: blessed is the Creator, the true King, who has set the whole world to its tasks. A mourning song that starts by praising the One who made the order the death belongs to. Later the alahnian say it plainly: whoever comes must rise and go. That's not cold comfort. It sets the grief inside the Creator's order instead of outside it, so the mourners aren't left alone with it. Put the two side by side. Both are about leaving: a groom leaves to begin a household; a soul leaves this world. Both are about a journey toward the Lord. And both are sung in Vadhans. The Gurus didn't need one sound for celebration and another for loss. The same music walks with a family through both doors.
screen: `GHORIAN: THE BODY IS THE MARE.` · `RIDING TOWARD THE LORD.` · `ALAHNIAN: BLESSED IS THE CREATOR.` · `WHOEVER COMES MUST GO.` · then, large: `THE SAME RAGA FOR BOTH.`

segments.voice: With each in-breath, think of a beginning you've witnessed, a wedding, a birth, a first day; with each out-breath, an ending, a goodbye, a funeral, a last visit, and notice it's one breath doing both. If you pray, say Waheguru at the turn of each breath. If an ending is still raw and heavier than you can carry, in the US you can call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.
A hymn in Vadhans. Guru Ram Das's wedding-horse song, where the body is the mare, and Guru Nanak's lament, which opens by blessing the Creator. Today's word.
Your line: the same raga for both. A body as the mare, and a lament that opens with blessed. Day one thousand eighty-one, done.

howItsDone: Guru Ram Das's ghorian and Guru Nanak's alahnian are both sung in Raga Vadhans; the ghorian are associated with weddings and the alahnian with mourning, and both turn the occasion toward remembrance of God.

chat.says: Why would a Sikh lament for the dead begin with the word 'blessed'?
options: It praises the Creator first, setting the loss inside God's order so mourners aren't alone.
It's a wedding word that slipped into the lament when the book was put together.
It's thanking the mourners who came, the way a host greets guests at the door.

notes: Ghorian (M4, Ang 575) paraphrased: the body is the mare the Lord created; blessed is the human body, gained by good fortune; saddled with the Guru's word, ridden toward the Lord. Please confirm the paraphrase and Ang.

Alahnian (M1) paraphrased: opening 'dhan sirandha sacha patisahu jin jag dhandhai laia' (blessed is the Creator, the true King, who set the world to its tasks) and 'baba aaia hai uth chalna' (whoever comes must rise and go). Please confirm Angs and that 'blessed' is a fair rendering of the opening word.
The hook's wedding and mourning scenes are illustrations, not claims about when these shabads are sung. howItsDone says 'associated with'; please confirm.
